https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/04/fere.text: Menü Kereső Budapest történelmének fontos darabját mutatja meg nekünk a rekordalacsony vízállású Duna Belföld Legfontosabb Az egykori Ferenc József híd maradványai láthatóak a Dunában a rendkívül alacsony vízállásnál a Szabadság híd alatt 2026. augusztus 4-én – Fotó: MTI Nagy Nikoletta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Egy héttel ezelőtt megdőlt a Duna vízállásának negatív rekordja Budapesten, akkor 30 centiméterre mérte az Országos Vízügyi Igazgatóság a vízszintet (ami persze nem azt jelenti, hogy csak 30 centi víz volt a folyóban, hanem a vízmérce nulla pontjához képest volt ennyi). A helyzet azóta kismértékben javult: a legfrissebb adatok szerint kedden délután négykor 16 centin járt a mutató. Ha valaki ebben az időszakban a Szabadság hídon jár, és lenéz a vízhiányos Dunára, érdekes látvány fogadja: a folyóban ugyanis látszanak az egykori Ferenc József híd maradványai. Ez a híd a mai a Szabadság híd elődje volt, és a németek robbantották bele a Dunába a második világháborúban (vagy nem, erről majd kicsit később). Bár a romok nagy részét a szovjetek a háború vége felé eltakarították, maradt még néhány hídelem, ami a Duna mélyén, a jelenlegi híddal párhuzamosan fekszik. Történt már egyébként korábban is ilyen: 2018-ban is nagyon kevés víz volt a Dunában, igaz, nem ennyire, hiszen akkor 32 centiméternél megállt az apadás. A Ferenc József híd akkor is előbukkant a hullámsírból. A híd annak idején Budapest harmadik közúti hídja volt, 1896-ban adták át, a millenniumi világkiállítás részeként épült szecessziós stílusban, turulokkal és az ország címerével díszítették. A nevét onnan kapta, hogy Ferenc József császár avatta fel, az utolsó ezüst szegecset ő maga verte be az építménybe. A Ferenc József híd budai hídfője 1926-ban – Fotó: Pesti Brúnó / Fortepan 49 évvel az építése után, 1945 januárjában robbantották fel. A közvélekedés szerint a visszavonuló német csapatok tették tönkre, de Ungváry Krisztián történész szerint ez nem biztos; akár a háború utáni magyar és szovjet propaganda által erőltetett narratíva is lehetett, hiszen a híd felrobbantásában a szovjet hadvezetés is érdekelt volt – olyannyira, hogy Sztálin maga adta ki a hidak elpusztítására vonatkozó parancsot. Január 16-án 22:15-kor a IX. SS-hegyihadtest azt táviratozta, hogy a Ferenc József hidat megsemmisítette egy bombatalálat. A támadások már korábban átlyukasztották a híd pályatestét, de az áthaladást nem tették teljesen lehetetlenné. A híd azért semmisült meg végül, mert egy szovjet aknatalálat – tehát nem a repülőbombák – berobbantotta a hídra a német utászok által fölszerelt robbantótöltetet is. A felrobbant híd 1945-ben – Fotó: Fortepan A Ferenc József híd középső hídnyílását szinte teljes egészében elnyelte a folyó, és a parti nyílások is károsodtak. A háború még tartott, amikor a szovjetek elkezdték elbontani a híd használhatatlan maradványait, és pontonhidat építettek a romokra. Ezt az 1945-ös januári jégzajlás tette tönkre. Aztán megkezdődött az új Szabadság híd építése a korábbi híd megmaradt és felhasználható szerkezeti elemein – ez volt az első híd a világháború után, amit újra felhúztak a Dunán. 1946 nyarán kezdődtek meg a munkálatok, és augusztus 20-án adták át újra a budapestieknek. Nem messze a mai Szabadság hídtól fekszik egyébként az úgynevezett Ínség-szikla is, ami akkor bukkan fel a vízből, amikor nagyon alacsony a Duna vízállása – innen ered a neve is. Lehet, hogy a Ferenc József hidat is lassan felvehetjük az aszályjelző tájképek listájára. Az újjáépített és átnevezett híd 1946. augusztus 20-án az átadáson – Fotó: Gara család / Fortepan Érdemes egyébként tudni, hogy a Gellért-hegy mai dunai oldala emberi munka eredménye, régen a folyó egészen a sziklák lábáig nyújtózott, és folyamatosan ostromolta az instabil hegyoldalt. A Dunai Szigetek blog szerint gyakoriak voltak az omlások, és emiatt óriási kőtömbök hevertek a folyó medrében. Ezen sziklák egyike az Ínség-szikla, de van még belőlük bőven: az egyik, a Szabadság hídtól délnyugatra található, nagyjából 60 méter hosszú sziklahát szembetűnően befolyásolja az áramlási viszonyokat. Ha az ember elnéz odáig a hídról, gyakran látszanak itt hatalmas örvények tölcsérei. A Ferenc József híd romjait szonárral is vizsgálták már , a felvételeken jól látszik, hogy hol helyezkedik el a törmelékhalmaz a Szabadság hídhoz képest. A roncsok jelentős részét már üledékréteg fedi, de egy kis darabjuk még kilóg a folyó iszapjából, erről lehet most szép képeket készíteni, ha valaki arra jár. Photograph: Marty Lederhandler/AP View image in fullscreen The twin towers of the World Trade Center burning behind the Empire State Building in New York on 9/11. Photograph: Marty Lederhandler/AP September 11 2001 ‘Institutional neglect’: 25 years on from 9/11, experts sound alarm over US counter-terror efforts Budget cuts, loss of knowledgeable officials and diverted resources raise risk of another attack, experts warn Jason Burke International security correspondent Thu 10 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US faces growing challenges in countering international terrorism as resources are diverted to other threats, experienced security officials leave and “complacency” spreads, experts have warned. It is 25 years this week since the 9/11 attacks launched by Osama bin Laden’s al-Qaida on New York and Washington, which killed about 3,000 people and led to decades of conflict, radicalisation and instability across the Middle East and beyond. Though there have been no successful attacks on anything like a similar scale in the US since, and only a small number inspired by extremist Islamist ideologies, many are warning of growing risks. Some blame Donald Trump for politicising counter-terrorism efforts, making ill-considered and inappropriate appointments to senior intelligence posts and diverting attention from more urgent threats with a campaign against drug cartels. View image in fullscreen Members of the Mexican national guard and army patrol the border wall between Mexico and the US. Trump has shifted focus and resources by designating criminal groups such as the Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organisations. Photograph: José Luis González/Reuters Bruce Hoffman, a terrorism expert at Georgetown University, said: “I remember [9/11] and this pure chaos and pandemonium in the streets and I remember thinking that we would never lower our guard again and complacency against a threat that is episodic but when it is revealed highly consequential.” This year, Hoffmann told the US House permanent select committee on intelligence that “the counter-terrorism architecture built after 9/11 is eroding … through budget cuts, personnel losses, and the diminution of terrorism as a national security priority”. This was “recreating the conditions of under-resourcing and institutional neglect that preceded the 2001 attacks. Moreover, the terrorist threat to Americans has both changed and grown.” Analysts are split over whether the lack of obvious recent efforts by al-Qaida to strike in the US suggests a lack of ambition or disguises a careful, strategic plan to wait for the right opportunity. Last month, a UN report based on intelligence supplied by member states’ monitoring said the “al-Qaida senior leadership remained marginalized” while “its capability and intent to conduct external operations remained unclear”. Colin Clarke, the executive director of the Soufan Center, said the US intelligence community was experiencing a “basket of factors” including “funding, personnel [and] complacency”. “There is a certain amount of fatigue. We did the global war on terror for 20 years and people were keen to pivot to something else,” he said. Most analysts support a 2018 shift away from terrorism to focus on “long-term, strategic competition by … revisionist powers” such as Russia and China. But choices made by the Trump administration have exacerbated existing problems. “There is a real lack of morale because of the way the president has treated the intelligence community … the quiet professionals are really demoralised,” Clarke said. View image in fullscreen Intelligence veterans criticised the appointments of Tulsi Gabbard and Kash Patel to high-profile national intelligence roles. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Intelligence veterans criticised the appointments of Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence and Kash Patel as director of the FBI, accusing both of lacking sufficient top-level experience in law enforcement. For the 2026 financial year, funding requested for the principal agencies of the civilian intelligence community totalled $81bn. But the designation of criminal groups such as the Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organisations has stretched resources. An updated counter-terrorism strategy released in May by the Trump administration has been controversial. Many intelligence experts and analysts have highlighted how the strategy downplays the rising threat from rightwing extremism in the US and stresses instead the battle against leftwing violence, cartels and gangs. “It is a very partial document [and] raises the question: are you protecting America or people who agree with you?” said Clarke. “We have finite resources now. You don’t have a blank cheque like after 9/11 and at the same time it’s not just Sunni jihadist groups which are considered the threat.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Thing Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Devorah Margolin at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy said that the new strategy was a significant shift. “That is not to say that counter-terrorism policies cannot change as the landscape changes, but this year’s strategy appears more focused on a political agenda than the reality of the threat,” Margolin added. View image in fullscreen People in lower Manhattan watch smoke billow from the World Trade Center on 9/11. One expert said the focus has shifted from terrorism to threats from China and Russia. Photograph: Amy Sancetta/AP “While the strategy still acknowledged the threat posed by groups like the Islamic State and al-Qaida, it also expanded definitions of counter-terrorism. It sought to use the vast counter-terrorism bureaucracy that has been built over the last two decades for its own political agenda. This has spread dwindling counter-terrorism resources even thinner.” The loss of experienced personnel is a significant problem, experts say, with many criticising the dismantlement last year of programmes aimed at countering extremist ideologies and preventing radicalisation. Don Rassler, the director of strategic initiatives at the Combating Terrorism Center at West Point, said that terrorism became less of a priority as strategic focus shifted to real or potential threats from China and Russia, and warned the US needed to be careful the intelligence community did not “revert back to the dynamics that led to an event like 9/11”. The 2001 attacks were the culmination of a series of attacks launched by Bin Laden on US targets. In 1996 and again in 1998, 10 years after founding al-Qaida, Bin Laden “declared war” on America with statements issued from a base in Afghanistan, listing grievances including US backing for “tyrannical, apostate” regimes in the Middle East such as in his native Saudi Arabia amid a broader diatribe against what he called western aggression against Muslims worldwide. Shortly afterwards, double bombings demolished two US embassies in east Africa and a suicide attack nearly sank a US warship off Yemen in 2000. The failure of senior officials including George W Bush to act on multiple intelligence warnings was highlighted by the congressional investigation into the 9/11 attacks, as well as the failure of the FBI and the CIA to share with each other vital information that might have prevented the atrocity. View image in fullscreen The Freedom Tower rises above one of the 9/11 memorial reflecting pools. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images An al-Qaida effort to blow up a passenger plane as it prepared to land in Detroit in 2009 was averted only at the last minute when explosives failed to detonate as intended. An attack a decade later by a single “self-radicalised” Saudi Arabian air force officer in Florida which killed three was linked to the organisation’s affiliate in Yemen. Since then, there have been more than 100 attacks in the US by violent Islamic extremists linked to the broader “jihadi” movement, according to a count by the Center for Strategic and International Studies . Rassler said extremist Islamist groups were still a key priority but with fewer resources and fewer people the US had “to accept more terrorist risk”. “There hasn’t been another attack … but there is a danger of believing that the [terrorist] threat isn’t there. The threat is different in many ways from 10 years ago and we have to be as clear-eyed as possible about it.” Explore more on these topics September 11 2001 Trump administration US politics features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/china-s-influence-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NVcB The Chinese game 'The Defiant' is set during the Second Sino-Japanese War Image: 4Divinity Advertisement In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees. Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s. Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game . Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese history Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW "The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles. Gaming is part of everyday life in China More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games . According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends. "Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users." 'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular games Image: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones , while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming. Limits on gaming time and extensive controls Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with. There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs , giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time. The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild" Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies. No license? No sales in China One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives. The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and Shanghai Image: Ubisoft The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says. Strict criteria for video games Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order. "The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion. Chinese culture is an international hit The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West." The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hit Image: Game Science Interactive Technology Co Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says. The problem of self-censorship Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?" He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship . That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities. China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika , may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions. History from a Chinese perspective Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history." Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge. This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal. https://www.irishtimes.com/world/europe/.text: Europe Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow Latvia's prime minister Andris Kulbergs and his wife Anna react after first exit poll results of the general election was announced. Photo: Wojtek Radwanski/ AFP/ Getty Sun Oct 04 2026 - 09:03 • 2 MIN READ Latvian prime minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro- Ukrainian coalition ‌after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991. With 97 per cent of ballots counted after Saturday’s election in the Nato ​and EU country bordering Russia , United List was on 35.3 per cent, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs (47), came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into ​Latvia. Latvia’s economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, ⁠political scientist Roberts Kits said. READ MORE Welcome to the new Global Briefing newsletter ‘Where is his authority?’ Germany is losing patience with Friedrich Merz After my friend lost his job, he asked AI what came next Raphaël Glucksmann’s refusal to use the word ‘genocide’ divides France’s left “Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that ‌he ‌can ​do things differently, bring some fresh energy,” he said. “This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains whether he has the team to do it.” United List ⁠appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with ​either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said. Kulbergs pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow. [ Latvians vote in election in shadow of drone incursions and war in Ukraine Opens in new window ] “Any ‌economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, ​it can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters at his party’s headquarters ⁠on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of ⁠the win. “It’s remarkably good. ​I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said. Election officials sort ballots at a polling station during elections for Latvia's 15th Parliament (Saeima) in Riga. Photo: Valda Kalnina/EPA Voter turnout was 51.8 per cent, down from 59.4 per cent in 2022. United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1 per cent. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7 per cent, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9 per cent. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5 per cent of gross domestic product, one of ‌the highest levels in Nato. His pro-Kremlin ⁠rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost of living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority. Latvia's prime minister Andris Kulbergs looks at his watch as he waits for the first exit poll results of the general election. Photo: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to ‌influence government policy. Latvia’s ethnic Russian minority is split between those who oppose Moscow’s war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed ​at limiting their influence on public life, which many of them see as discriminatory. Latvia, with ​a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and Nato allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. - Reuters Understand world events with Denis Staunton's Global Briefing newsletter Join The Irish Times on WhatsApp and stay up to date Listen to In The News podcast daily for a deep dive on the stories that matter Latvia EU North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) Ukraine crisis IN THIS SECTION Historic town hall torched and more than 1,200 arrested as protests spread across France Pope Leo leaves hospital after lung cancer surgery Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold amid deepening row with Ukraine Thousands march in Albanian capital as anti-government protests spread Zelenskiy no longer willing to placate Trump MOST READ Niamh Flatley: Riverdance star who played leading role in troupe’s global success Met Éireann in scramble to save amateur weather watchers’ network from shutdown US group buys largest Irish GP practice network in deal worth about €350m ‘I feel so grateful’: Fine Gael MEP Maria Walsh announces birth of child after fertility treatment Mark Zuckerberg drinks pint wrong, leaving his Irish reputation in tatters LATEST STORIES ‘Like being a shit celebrity’: Inside the world of top-level football referees Lara Gillespie wins gold at track cycling world championships Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer Human resources doesn’t need to be the CIA Trump will take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions, Rubio says
